goal: Ship the notes-cli single-user, offline note-taking CLI by choosing a storage approach for its note data, unblocking the TODO in src/notes/cli.py that blocks the milestone.
question: Select the storage approach for notes-cli's note data that best fits a single-user, fully offline Python CLI (>= 3.10) that currently has no third-party dependencies.
known_constraints: notes-cli runs entirely offline on the user's own machine; no network access is required or desired (README.md)
notes-cli is single-user and only one process touches the data at a time (README.md)
The project currently declares no third-party dependencies and targets Python >= 3.10 (pyproject.toml)

evidence: README.md describes notes-cli as a single-user note-taking CLI that runs entirely offline on the user's own machine, with no network access required or desired, and only one process touching the data at a time.
pyproject.toml declares dependencies = [] and requires-python >= 3.10, with the console script notes = notes.cli:main.
src/notes/cli.py lines 7-10 state the storage backend is not chosen and the TODO blocks the milestone.

A local runtime check at decision time (2026-10-01) confirmed Python 3.14.7 ships json, sqlite3 (bundled SQLite 3.53.4), and pathlib as standard-library modules under /usr/lib/python3.14; all import successfully with no third-party installation (python3 -c 'import json, sqlite3, pathlib').

alternatives.name: Single JSON file
alternatives.description: Persist all notes as a list of note objects in one JSON file (for example ~/.notes/notes.json) that the CLI reads and rewrites using the standard-library json module.
advantages: Uses only the Python standard library (json, pathlib); adds no dependency
The whole data file is human-readable and trivially inspectable, hand-editable, backed up, or version-controlled
Implementation is minimal: load the list, modify it, dump it back
Data lives in a single file, making backup and migration to another machine a file copy
disadvantages: Every command rewrites the entire file, and cost grows with the note corpus
No indexed queries; search scans the fully parsed list in memory
A naive write is not atomic, so an interrupted write can corrupt the file unless extra handling is added
No schema enforcement or type validation beyond ad-hoc checks in code
assumptions: The note corpus stays small enough to load fully into memory
Single-process access means no concurrent writers need guarding

alternatives.name: SQLite database file
alternatives.description: Store notes in a single SQLite database file accessed through Python's built-in sqlite3 module, with a notes table and parameterized SQL queries.
advantages: sqlite3 is in the Python standard library with a bundled SQLite engine; no third-party package and no server process
Transactional, atomic writes with rollback protect the data if a command is interrupted
Indexed queries and full-text search (FTS5) scale to large corpora without loading everything into memory
Column types and schema are enforced by the engine rather than by ad-hoc code
disadvantages: The data file is binary; reading or editing it requires the CLI or a SQLite tool
SQL statements and connection handling add implementation surface beyond plain file I/O
Schema changes over time must be handled as migrations
Version-control diffs of the data file are not meaningful
assumptions: A local single-file SQLite database satisfies the offline, single-machine requirement
The sqlite3 module is present in every Python environment the project supports

alternatives.name: Markdown file per note
alternatives.description: Store each note as its own Markdown or plain-text file with a small metadata header inside one notes directory, discovered and read with pathlib.
advantages: Uses only the Python standard library (pathlib, built-in open)
Every note is directly human-readable, hand-editable, and works with editors, grep, and version control
One file per note makes per-note export, selective backup, and sync natural
Deleting or renaming a note is a plain file operation
disadvantages: Listing and searching require directory traversal and per-file reads, which slow as the corpus grows
Metadata such as timestamps and tags lives in ad-hoc headers with no schema enforcement
File naming requires careful handling of collisions, Unicode, and length limits
Multi-file updates cannot be made atomic across files
assumptions: Users benefit from reading or editing note files directly with other tools
The corpus stays in a range where directory scans remain fast enough

criteria.name: Implementation simplicity
rubric: Requires a server or a new heavyweight dependency
Considerable boilerplate plus migration machinery to maintain
Moderate extra handling such as transactions or per-file bookkeeping

criteria.name: Query and scale capability
rubric: Full-file or full-scan search that degrades quickly with corpus size
Scan-based search workable for small corpora only
Indexed queries and full-text search that scale to large corpora

criteria.name: Data integrity
rubric: An interrupted write can silently corrupt stored data
Atomic per-file writes only; multi-file updates can tear
Atomic single-file writes with transactional rollback

criteria.name: Human readability and portability
rubric: Opaque binary format that needs tooling to read
Structured text that is machine-first but inspectable
Plain text directly readable, editable, and diff-friendly

criteria.name: Dependency footprint
rubric: Adds third-party packages or a server process

hard_constraints.description: All note data must be stored locally on the user's own machine and the CLI must operate entirely offline with no network access (README.md: "no network access is required or desired").
The storage approach must suit a single-user CLI where only one process touches the data at a time, and must not require a shared server or concurrent multi-process coordination (README.md).
